q: An adult who believes 'I was a kid once, so I know what kids are going through' and fails to set boundaries shows:
o: Overidentification
Underidentification
Countertransference resistance
Radical acceptance
e: Overidentification is assuming you understand children because you were once a child, and as a result failing to set appropriate boundaries or seeing your own childhood in theirs. Underidentification is the opposite: seeing children as alien beings, talking about a child as if they weren't present, and becoming condescending and rigid. Effective child interviewers avoid both extremes.
w: Underidentification is the opposite error: treating children as alien and becoming rigid.
Countertransference resistance isn't the term for this pattern.
Radical acceptance is a technique for welcoming client comments, not an interviewer error.
k: Overidentification ('I was a kid, I know') blurs boundaries; underidentification treats kids as alien.
h: Too close or too far: both miss the child.

q: The authors encourage professionals to view work with children as a form of:
o: Cross-cultural counseling
Family systems therapy only
Behavioral training
Educational consultation with schools
e: The authors encourage viewing work with children as a form of cross-cultural counseling: children inhabit a different culture, with their own language, values and ways of seeing the world. Like any cross-cultural work, it requires knowledge (developmental theory), real exposure to children, and awareness of your own reactions and assumptions.
w: Family systems therapy is one approach, not the overall frame the authors recommend.
Behavioural training is a technique, not the lens for understanding children.
Educational consultation is a role with schools, not how the authors frame child work.
k: Treat work with children as cross-cultural counseling: their world differs from adults'.

q: Which is described as a danger sign for child interviewers?
o: Fantasies about adopting or rescuing children in hard circumstances
Feeling genuine affection toward children and enjoying their company
Knowing developmental theory better than the practical side of childhood
Enjoying play
e: A danger sign for child interviewers is fantasizing about adopting or rescuing children in hard circumstances. Such overinvolvement can blur boundaries and serve the interviewer's needs rather than the child's. Overinvolvers need self-understanding, and other outlets for rescue needs, before doing therapeutic work with children.
w: Genuine affection for children is healthy and helps rapport.
Strong theory with less practical experience is a gap to fill, not a danger sign.
Enjoying play is an asset in child work.
k: Rescue or adoption fantasies are a danger sign of overinvolvement with child clients.

q: Why must balance be especially maintained with children?
o: They're vulnerable and usually can't leave or advocate in poor relationships
They are more resistant than adults and need firmer limits from the interviewer
They need less confidentiality
They always respond to authority, so the interviewer can easily overpower them
e: Balance between involvement and distance is especially important with children because they are vulnerable and usually can't leave a poor relationship or advocate for themselves. Children also push adults' buttons and trigger unfinished business from the interviewer's own childhood, while being less able to defend themselves against an interviewer's mistakes.
w: Children aren't necessarily more resistant; their vulnerability is the issue.
Children still need confidentiality, with clear limits.
Children don't always respond to authority, and overpowering them isn't the goal.
k: Children can't easily leave or advocate in poor relationships, so interviewers must keep balance.
h: They can't walk out, so you must stay balanced.

q: How do most young people come to mental health services?
o: Referred by parents, guardians, caretakers or school personnel
By calling a mental health professional themselves when distressed
Through internet searches
Through court orders only, after legal problems at school or home
e: Most young people are referred to mental health services by parents, guardians, caretakers or school personnel, not by themselves. As a result, they may not know whom they'll meet, why they're there, or even that they had an appointment. The interviewer must explain and engage from the start.
w: Children rarely self-refer; adults usually bring them.
Internet searches aren't how most youth arrive.
Court orders apply to some youth, but most are referred by parents or schools.
k: Most youth are referred by caretakers or schools, often without knowing why they're coming.

q: An interviewer who meets alone with caretakers first risks:
o: Being seen by an adolescent as the caretakers' agent
Breaking confidentiality laws that protect all minors
Losing the parents' trust because they feel judged by you
Nothing at any age
e: Meeting alone with caretakers first can make an adolescent see the interviewer as the caretakers' agent, damaging trust. This is much less of a concern with a 5-year-old. But not meeting caretakers separately also has problems, such as inappropriate disclosures in front of the child or angry parents. Plan the sequence deliberately.
w: It doesn't break confidentiality laws; the concern is perceived allegiance.
The usual risk is the teen's distrust, not parents feeling judged.
There is a risk, especially with adolescents.
k: Meeting parents first risks a teen seeing you as the parents' agent; plan the order.
h: Talk to Mom first, and the teen thinks you're Mom's spy.

q: In the Sandy Smith case, what did the counselor do when the father asked to talk alone first?
o: Warmly invited everyone in, promising to address his concerns later
Agreed and met with him alone, since he was paying for the counseling
Asked the father to leave so Sandy would feel safe and respected first
Met only with Sandy
e: When Sandy's father asked to talk alone first, the counselor warmly invited everyone in together, promising to address his concerns later. Without a clear plan and some assertiveness, an intimidating family member may take control of the interview and the treatment plan. Structure protects the child and the process.
w: Payment doesn't give the father control of the interview structure.
Asking the father to leave would alienate him.
Meeting only with Sandy would exclude important family input.
k: Keep control of the interview structure; don't let an intimidating parent dictate it.

q: If you plan individual therapy with a child, the child must realize that:
o: Your primary allegiance is to him or her
The parents control the therapy and its goals
The school will receive all details of each session
Confidentiality doesn't apply to minors under state law
e: In individual therapy, the child must understand that your primary allegiance is to them, not to their parents or school. Clarify caretakers' roles early, even during scheduling calls (Stone, 2005). Without this, children may see you as an extension of the adults who referred them.
w: Parents don't control therapy and its goals in individual work.
Schools don't receive session details; the child's communications stay confidential within limits.
Confidentiality does apply to minors, with limits.
k: In individual therapy, the child must know your primary allegiance is to them.

q: The Mrs. Piggle-Wiggle quote illustrates that:
o: Young people quickly sense whether professionals like and enjoy them
Children need strict rules before any relationship can develop
Food is the best rapport builder
Toys and games matter more than relationships
e: The Mrs. Piggle-Wiggle quote illustrates that young people quickly sense whether professionals genuinely like and enjoy them. If youth don't feel liked or respected, they're less likely to open up or keep coming. Authentic warmth and enjoyment of children are central to rapport.
w: Strict rules first isn't the point of the quote.
Food can help, but the quote is about genuine liking.
Relationships matter more than toys; the quote is about feeling liked.
k: Children quickly sense whether you truly like and enjoy them.

q: Children, even when cooperative, are best considered:
o: Involuntary clients – so offer them creative choices
Voluntary clients who chose to come to counseling themselves
Collateral informants about their parents' problems at home
Co-therapists in a family systems approach
e: Even when cooperative, children are best considered involuntary clients: adults decided they'd come. Offering creative choices restores some control: pick two toys to bring along, or choose which of three topics to discuss first. Small choices build cooperation and respect.
w: Children rarely choose counseling themselves; adults usually decide.
Children are clients, not collateral informants.
Children aren't co-therapists; they are the clients being helped.
k: Treat children as involuntary clients and offer them small, real choices.

q: What do the authors say about offering food to young clients?
o: Feeding young people builds relationship – even Freud fed hungry clients
It is always unethical, since it creates a dual relationship
It should only be candy
It replaces the need for rapport building during the first session
e: The authors note that feeding young people builds relationship; even Freud fed hungry clients. Snacks are especially useful after school. They avoid caffeine and sugary foods, though some therapists use them with parental permission. Food signals care and makes the setting more welcoming.
w: Offering food isn't automatically unethical; it can build relationship.
Candy isn't recommended; healthier snacks are preferred.
Food supports rapport but doesn't replace it.
k: Offering (healthy) food builds relationship with young clients.

q: Why is it better to let young clients notice office items on their own?
o: Exploring builds comfort, and their reactions provide assessment data
Children shouldn't touch anything without permission
It prevents breakage of the counselor's expensive toys and art supplies
It saves time
e: Letting young clients notice and explore office items on their own builds comfort, and their reactions provide assessment data about interests, maturity and needs. For example, teens may mock stuffed animals, but this mockery likely covers comfort and dependency needs they don't want to admit.
w: Children can explore; rigid rules about touching hinder comfort.
Preventing breakage isn't the main reason.
Saving time isn't the reason; comfort and assessment are.
k: Let kids explore office items: it builds comfort and reveals information.
h: What they pick up tells you something.

q: Why might a suit and tie hinder rapport with oppositional adolescents?
o: It may signal a rigid authority figure, triggering transference
Teens actually prefer formal therapists
It is considered unprofessional attire in most child clinics
It distracts from toys
e: With oppositional adolescents, a suit and tie may signal a rigid authority figure, triggering transference from conflicts with parents, teachers or police. More casual attire is generally recommended for work with teens. Adolescents even compare notes on their 'shrinks', so appearance shapes your reputation and first impressions.
w: Oppositional teens generally don't prefer formal therapists.
Suits aren't unprofessional; they're just less engaging for teens.
Distracting from toys isn't the issue.
k: Formal attire can trigger authority transference in oppositional teens; dress more casually.

q: In the recommended confidentiality explanation, what will parents receive?
o: General progress reports only, unless something dangerous comes up
Detailed copies of the session notes after every appointment
Nothing at all, ever
Whatever the child says about them
e: In the recommended confidentiality explanation, parents receive general progress reports only, unless something dangerous comes up. If it does, everyone will be brought together to talk directly. The limits of confidentiality are danger to self or others and child abuse.
w: Detailed session notes would destroy the child's trust.
Parents do get general progress reports, so 'nothing ever' is wrong.
Sharing whatever the child says about parents breaches confidentiality.
k: Parents get general progress reports only, unless danger arises.

q: When both parents and the minor sign informed consent documents, this is called:
o: Parental consent and child assent
Dual consent and dual confidentiality
Joint confidentiality agreement
Guardian authorization and release
e: When both parents and the minor sign informed consent documents, it's called parental consent and child assent: parents give legal consent, and the child agrees. Decide beforehand if, when and how you'll inform parents about a teen's dangerous behaviour, since laws vary by state.
w: Dual consent and dual confidentiality isn't the term.
Joint confidentiality agreement isn't the term.
Guardian authorization and release isn't the term.
k: Parents give legal consent; the minor gives assent to treatment.

q: Leve (1995) argues that telling children their words will be kept in confidence:
o: Signals rare respect and makes therapy feel uniquely important
Confuses children, who expect adults to share everything with parents
Is unnecessary under age 12, since parents hold all of the legal rights
Undermines parents
e: Leve (1995) argues that telling children their words will be kept confidential signals a rare kind of respect from an adult, making therapy feel uniquely important. Children seldom experience adults keeping their confidences. Talk about confidentiality and its limits with children of all ages.
w: Children aren't confused by it; they feel respected.
It's useful even under age 12.
It doesn't undermine parents when limits are explained.
k: Leve: promising confidentiality shows children rare respect and makes therapy special.
h: A secret kept is respect shown.

q: According to Wax (2001), about what share of U.S. children are children of immigrants?
o: One in five
One in ten
One in three
One in twenty
e: Wax (2001) reports that about one in five U.S. children are children of immigrants. Don't assume immigrant families suffer from bicultural demands; gently ask about language and culture at home, for example 'Do you speak Russian or English at home?', and let the family describe its experience.
w: One in ten understates the figure.
One in three overstates the figure.
One in twenty understates the figure.
k: About one in five U.S. children are children of immigrants (Wax, 2001).

q: Telling a child exactly why he or she was referred is what the authors call:
o: Acknowledging reality
Radical acceptance
Role induction for youth
Externalizing the problem
e: Telling a child exactly why they were referred is what the authors call acknowledging reality. Keeping referral secrets harms the relationship, and the referral source isn't your primary client. Warn referral sources first that you'll share the reasons with the child.
w: Radical acceptance is welcoming client comments.
Role induction explains how therapy works, not why the child was referred.
Externalizing the problem treats it as separate from the child.
k: Tell children openly why they were referred ('acknowledging reality').
h: No secrets about why you're here.

q: When reviewing referral information with an adolescent, the interviewer in the example:
o: Sat alongside the client, read it together, and checked in on each item
Read it aloud from across the room
Gave it to the parents to summarize for the adolescent at home later
Kept it secret
e: In the example, the interviewer sat alongside the adolescent, read the referral information together, and checked in on each item. Screen especially negative information first, and empathize with the client's feelings without endorsing negative behaviours. Reading together signals transparency and partnership.
w: Reading aloud from across the room feels distant and judgmental.
Having parents summarize it removes transparency.
Keeping the referral information secret harms trust and transparency.
k: Review referral information side by side with the teen, checking in on each item.
h: Read it together, side by side.

q: Which is listed as a common referral reason for preschool to latency-age children?
o: Enuresis or encopresis
Eating disorders
Juvenile probation mandate
Substance abuse
e: Common referral reasons for preschool to latency-age children include enuresis or encopresis, moodiness or aggression, unusual fears, precocious sexual behaviour, trauma, hyperactivity or inattention (mostly boys), and custody battles. Eating disorders, probation and substance abuse are more typical of adolescence.
w: Eating disorders typically emerge in adolescence.
Juvenile probation applies to older youth.
Substance abuse is typical of adolescence.
k: Young children's referrals: enuresis/encopresis, aggression, fears, trauma, hyperactivity, custody issues.
h: Wetting and soiling are early-childhood referrals.

q: In the goals statement used with families, who is asked to answer first?
o: The youngest person in the room
The parent who made the phone call
The father, as head of the family
The oldest sibling present
e: When asking families 'If you came to counseling and your life got better, what would change?', the youngest person in the room answers first, so they aren't overshadowed or simply echo the adults. This is used with children over 6; with children 6 and younger, meet with parents separately.
w: The parent who called often speaks first, which can drown out the child.
Asking the father first reinforces hierarchy.
The oldest sibling isn't chosen first.
k: Ask the youngest family member to answer the goals question first.

q: The three-wishes question structures goals into which categories?
o: Self-change, family change, school change
Past, present, and future wishes
Thoughts, feelings, and behaviors to change
Friends, family members, and the wider community
e: The three-wishes question structures goals into self-change, family change and school change. If a client resists, the interviewer can amplify playfully ('maybe I should change places with you'), then allow a pass. The wishes reveal the child's perspective and family dynamics.
w: Past, present and future isn't the structure.
Thoughts, feelings and behaviours isn't the structure.
Friends, family and community isn't the structure.
k: Three wishes: one for self-change, one for family change, one for school change.

q: A child wishes for parents and school to change but admits no personal problems. This pattern is typical of:
o: Disruptive behavior disorders (ADHD, ODD, CD)
Internalizing disorders (anxiety, depression, worry)
Autism spectrum disorders
Adjustment disorders
e: A child who wishes for parents and school to change but admits no personal problems shows a pattern typical of disruptive behaviour disorders (ADHD, ODD, conduct disorder), which tend to externalize. Children with internalizing disorders, such as anxiety and depression, tend to identify their own shortcomings ('I'd like to be happier').
w: Internalizing disorders involve self-focused wishes like 'be happier'.
Autism spectrum disorders aren't characterized by this pattern.
Adjustment disorders aren't defined by this wish pattern.
k: Wishing only for others to change suggests externalizing (disruptive behaviour) disorders.

q: During joint sessions, parents' negative comments about the child should usually be limited to about:
o: Three problem statements
Just one
About ten
No limit at all, so parents feel heard
e: In joint sessions, limit parents' negative comments about the child to about three problem statements, so the child isn't overwhelmed or shamed. Invite parents to write further concerns, ask for the child's strengths, or meet separately later with the child's permission.
w: One problem statement may leave parents feeling unheard.
Ten problem statements can overwhelm and shame the child.
No limit risks a long, damaging list of complaints.
k: Limit parents' negative comments in joint sessions to about three problems.

q: If, after help and humor, a young client still can't identify any personal goal, the authors suggest:
o: The therapy prognosis may not be promising
The child has no real problems after all
Diagnose oppositional defiant disorder at intake
End therapy immediately and refer to a specialist
e: If, even after help and humour, a young client can't identify any personal goal, the therapy prognosis may not be promising, since change needs some personal investment. Still, children's wishes about their parents are crucial assessment information and reveal family dynamics.
w: The child may still have real problems.
Diagnosing ODD from this alone is premature.
Ending therapy immediately isn't the recommendation.
k: No personal goal, even after help, suggests a less promising prognosis.

q: In Baumrind-based parenting styles, Coloroso's 'backbone' parents correspond to:
o: Authoritative – highly demanding and highly responsive
Autocratic parents – rules etched in stone, my way only
Permissive parents – warm, flexible and accepting
Unengaged parents – letting children grow up freely on their own
e: Coloroso's parenting types map onto Baumrind's styles. 'Backbone' parents are authoritative: highly demanding and highly responsive, firm yet flexible. 'Brickwall' parents are autocratic ('my way or the highway'), 'jellyfish' parents are permissive (children rule the house), and unengaged parents leave children to raise themselves.
w: Autocratic parents are Coloroso's 'brickwall' type.
Permissive parents are Coloroso's 'jellyfish' type.
Unengaged parents leave children to raise themselves.
k: Backbone = authoritative; brickwall = autocratic; jellyfish = permissive.
h: Backbone bends and holds; brickwall never bends; jellyfish has no spine.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – Assessing parents or caretakers

q: When parents show mildly unhealthy patterns in the first session, the usual recommendation is:
o: Wait for more rapport before feedback; parents are often defensive
Confront the patterns immediately to protect the child
Report the parents to child protective services as a precaution
Refuse to continue
e: When parents show mildly unhealthy patterns in a first session, the usual recommendation is to wait for more rapport before giving feedback, because parents are often defensive and may feel blamed for their child's problems. Options range from waiting, to gentle feedback, to further assessment, to reporting abuse if legally required.
w: Immediate confrontation tends to make parents defensive and may end treatment.
Mildly unhealthy patterns don't meet the threshold for a protective services report.
Refusing to continue abandons the child and family.
k: Mildly unhealthy parenting early on: build rapport before offering feedback.

q: A parent says, 'I believe in giving my kid a swat.' The radical acceptance response is:
o: 'I'm very glad you brought up the topic of spanking.'
'Spanking is harmful to children and it must stop right now.'
'Let's not discuss discipline methods here today.'
'I'll have to report that to child protective services.'
e: Radical acceptance means welcoming even concerning statements: 'I'm very glad you brought up the topic of spanking.' Once unhealthy beliefs are exposed and affirmed as discussable, they may 'shrink, melt, crumble'. This parallels DBT and ACT: 'I accept you as you are, and I am helping you to change.'
w: Declaring spanking harmful immediately shuts down discussion and invites defensiveness.
Avoiding the topic loses the chance to work on discipline.
A swat alone isn't automatically reportable; threatening a report destroys trust.
k: Radical acceptance welcomes concerning beliefs so they can be explored and changed.
h: Welcome it in so it can melt.

q: Parents who scold misbehavior and ignore good behavior are, behaviorally:
o: Positively reinforcing misbehavior and extinguishing good behavior
Using effective punishment that reliably reduces misbehavior over time
Using negative reinforcement correctly to shape compliance
Applying differential reinforcement of alternative, incompatible behaviors
e: Parents who scold misbehaviour and ignore good behaviour are, behaviourally, positively reinforcing misbehaviour, because attention is a reward, and extinguishing good behaviour, because it gets no response. Assess family contingencies by observing parent–child interactions and asking each person separately what happens next during typical conflicts.
w: Scolding can act as attention that reinforces misbehaviour, not effective punishment.
Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant; that isn't what's happening.
Differential reinforcement would reward good behaviour, which these parents ignore.
k: Scolding misbehaviour and ignoring good behaviour reinforces the bad and extinguishes the good.

q: How do the authors respond to parents who equate positive reinforcement with bribery?
o: Bribery is 'paying someone in advance to do something illegal'; reinforcement works better
Agree that it is bribery and recommend consistent punishment for any misbehavior instead
Avoid the topic
Recommend ignoring all behavior, positive and negative, until the child settles down
e: When parents call positive reinforcement bribery, the authors note that bribery is 'paying someone in advance to do something illegal', while reinforcement rewards desirable behaviour after it occurs, and it works better. Asking parents about the reinforcements they receive in their own lives, like a paycheck, helps (Maag, 2001).
w: Agreeing and recommending punishment misses that reinforcement is more effective.
Avoiding the topic leaves an obstacle to effective parenting.
Ignoring all behaviour removes the reinforcement good behaviour needs.
k: Reinforcement isn't bribery: bribery pays in advance for wrongdoing; reinforcement rewards good behaviour after.
h: Do you call your paycheck a bribe?

q: In the 'What's good about you?' game, the question is asked:
o: 10 times, with a different answer each time
3 times
5 times, then 'What's bad about you?' 10 times
Until the child stops answering
e: In the 'What's good about you?' game, the interviewer asks the question 10 times, requiring a different answer each time, and responds 'Thank you' with a smile. 'I don't know' can be used only once. 'What's bad about you?' is asked only five times, keeping the balance positive.
w: Three times is too few for the game.
Five times is the number for 'What's bad about you?', not the positive question.
There's a set number, not 'until the child stops'.
k: 'What's good about you?': asked 10 times, new answer each time; 'bad' only 5 times.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – What's good (bad) about you?

q: A youth answers 'I have a nice bike' and 'I am a good son.' According to the authors, this may suggest:
o: Less adequate self-esteem – naming possessions or roles, not attributes
Excellent self-esteem grounded in strong relationships
Conduct disorder, since the answers avoid personal responsibility
Grandiosity
e: Naming possessions ('I have a nice bike') or roles ('I am a good son') rather than personal attributes may suggest less adequate self-esteem. Stating attributes, such as 'I'm a good bike rider' or 'I'm thoughtful with my parents', is probably evidence of more adequate self-esteem, because worth is located in the self.
w: Possessions and roles don't indicate excellent self-esteem.
Avoiding responsibility isn't the interpretation given.
Naming a bike isn't grandiose; it points to possessions rather than qualities.
k: Naming possessions or roles instead of attributes may suggest weaker self-esteem.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – What's good about you?

q: What should interviewers do when a child asks to switch roles and ask them 'What's good about you?'
o: Comply – it models and empowers the child
Refuse, in order to maintain professional boundaries
End the game
Interpret the request as a sign of manipulation
e: When a child asks to switch roles and ask the interviewer 'What's good about you?', comply. Answering models healthy self-appreciation and empowers the child by sharing control of the game. Youth with conduct disorder may ridicule the procedure, but most other children enjoy it and engage more fully afterwards.
w: Refusing feels rigid and misses a chance to model.
Ending the game punishes the child's engagement and curiosity.
Wanting to switch isn't manipulation; it's often healthy curiosity.
k: If a child wants to switch roles in the strengths game, comply: it models and empowers.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – What's good about you?

q: Projective drawings (Draw-A-Person, Kinetic Family Drawing, House-Tree-Person) should be used for:
o: Stimulating conversation, generating hypotheses and building rapport
Concluding whether abuse has occurred, based on drawing content
Diagnosing personality disorders precisely
Measuring IQ
e: Projective drawings such as Draw-A-Person, Kinetic Family Drawing and House-Tree-Person are criticized as unreliable, but they have high practical utility with youth for stimulating conversation, generating hypotheses and building rapport. Never use them to conclude that child sexual abuse occurred, because drawing content can't establish what happened.
w: Drawings can't establish whether abuse occurred.
They aren't reliable enough to diagnose personality disorders.
They don't measure IQ; standardized tests do.
k: Projective drawings: use for conversation, hypotheses and rapport, never to prove abuse.
h: Draw to talk, not to diagnose.

q: The most common single rule stated in a child's play session is:
o: It's not okay to break things or hurt yourself or anyone else
Stay seated at all times unless told otherwise
Speak only when asked a question by the counselor
Don't touch any toys without asking for permission first
e: The most common single rule in a child's play session: it's not okay to break things or hurt yourself or anyone else. In assessment, fewer rules allow freer expression, but plan for limit setting in advance: 'fail to plan… plan to fail.'
w: Requiring the child to stay seated restricts play.
Speaking only when asked defeats the purpose of play.
Asking permission for every toy limits free expression.
k: Core play rule: no breaking things and no hurting yourself or others.

q: Why is cleanup time valuable?
o: It reveals how the child handles endings and relates to you
It protects the toys and keeps the office ready for the next client
It teaches responsibility and good habits that transfer to home
It shortens the session
e: Cleanup time is valuable assessment data: it reveals how the child handles endings and relates to you. Watch for abrupt shifts toward toys, refusal to clean up, or frantic cleaning to impress the interviewer. Each pattern says something about transitions, authority and approval.
w: Protecting toys is practical but not the clinical value.
Teaching habits isn't the main point in assessment.
It doesn't shorten the session; it's part of it.
k: Cleanup time reveals how the child handles endings and relates to you.
h: How they end is how they leave.

q: Which art modality is described as the 'loosest' and potentially producing the most emotional looseness?
o: Finger-painting
Colored pencils
Drawing pencils
Collage building
e: Finger-painting is the loosest art modality and can produce the most emotional looseness. Looser, wetter modalities elicit more emotion and may stimulate loss of self-control, while colored pencils and drawing pencils are more controlled. Choose the medium based on how much emotional expression the child can handle.
w: Colored pencils are among the most controlled media.
Drawing pencils are controlled, not loose.
Collage is structured, not the loosest.
k: Finger-painting is the loosest modality; pencils are the most controlled.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – Putting It in Practice 12.1

q: With self-conscious adolescents who are drawing, the interviewer should generally:
o: Keep busy with a drawing of your own rather than hovering
Watch closely and comment on each line as it is being drawn
Leave the room
Correct the drawing gently so the teen learns proper technique
e: With self-conscious adolescents who are drawing, keep busy with a drawing of your own rather than hovering over them, which reduces their sense of being watched and evaluated. With younger children, watching with a few supportive, nondirective comments may be appropriate, since they usually welcome adult attention to their work.
w: Watching closely and commenting increases self-consciousness.
Leaving the room abandons the shared activity.
Correcting technique turns therapy into an art lesson.
k: With self-conscious teens, draw alongside them instead of watching.

q: In Cary's case (12-year-old with elderly parents and frail grandparents), what did the collage reveal?
o: A longing for a 'normal' family with young parents and healthy grandparents
Anger at his school and teachers for the slipping grades he received
Strong interest in sports and in the friends he had stopped seeing lately
Desire to move out
e: Cary, 12, with elderly parents and frail grandparents, said he accepted his family, but his collage of young parents and upbeat words revealed a longing for a 'normal' family with young parents and healthy grandparents, along with grief. This guided the treatment plan beyond his verbal account.
w: Anger at school wasn't what the collage showed.
Sports interest wasn't the collage's message.
A desire to move out wasn't the theme.
k: Art can reveal feelings words hide: Cary's collage showed longing and grief.
h: The collage said what he couldn't.

q: Virginia Axline, author of Dibs, advocated:
o: Nondirective, minimally interactive play therapy
Directive behavioral play with clear rewards and limits
Sand tray therapy as the central treatment modality
Storytelling and mutual storytelling only
e: Virginia Axline, author of Dibs: In Search of Self, advocated nondirective, minimally interactive play therapy, based on person-centered principles: the child leads, the therapist reflects and accepts. Other approaches use play to enhance relationships and explore themes, or more directively to teach empathy and adaptive behaviour.
w: Directive behavioural play is a different approach.
Sand tray therapy isn't what Axline advocated.
Storytelling techniques are associated with others, such as Gardner.
k: Virginia Axline (Dibs) advocated nondirective, minimally interactive play therapy.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – Nondirective, interactive and directive play

q: Which caution applies to construction sets like Legos?
o: Avoid with small children who might swallow pieces; beware with violent ones
They are always safe, since the pieces are too small
They are only for adolescents
They require specialized art therapy training before use in sessions
e: Construction sets like Legos need caution in the playroom: avoid them with small children who might swallow pieces, and be careful with violent or aggressive children, since small hard pieces can easily become weapons. Choose play materials deliberately, based on the child's age, developmental level and behaviour.
w: Small pieces are a choking hazard, not safe for all ages.
They aren't only for adolescents; age matters because of choking risk.
They don't require specialized art therapy training.
k: Legos: choking risk for small children and possible weapons for violent ones.

q: What is the authors' position on anatomically accurate dolls?
o: Useful, but require training and supervision given the controversy
They prove that abuse occurred whenever children use them sexually
They should never be used, because they plant ideas in children's minds
Any interviewer can use them
e: Anatomically accurate dolls can be useful, but they require specialized training and supervision given the controversy around them. Concrete interpretations of sexual doll play became controversial (Dickinson et al.; Faller; Hungerford), because doll play alone can't establish that abuse occurred and untrained use can mislead investigations.
w: Sexual doll play doesn't prove abuse.
They aren't banned; they need training.
Untrained interviewers shouldn't use them, given the controversy.
k: Anatomically accurate dolls: potentially useful, but only with training and supervision.

q: Up to about what age will young children comply and answer a question they don't understand?
o: About age nine
About age four
About age twelve
About age six
e: Up to about age nine, young children tend to comply and answer questions they don't understand, wanting to please adults or assuming there must be an answer. Even 4-year-olds can be reliable reporters, but interviewers may inadvertently coerce responses through leading, repeated or confusing questions.
w: Age four understates; compliance extends to about nine.
Age twelve overstates the typical range.
Age six understates the range; it extends to about nine.
k: Until about age 9, children may answer questions they don't understand.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – Putting It in Practice 12.2

q: Which approaches tend to be most effective for gathering accurate information from children?
o: Open-ended prompts and cued invitations, practiced on neutral events
Leading yes/no questions, which young children can answer more easily
Repeated direct questions until the child gives a consistent, clear answer
Multiple-choice questions
e: Open-ended prompts and cued invitations ('Tell me more about…'), practised first on neutral events, are most effective for gathering accurate information from children. Leading, repeated or multiple-choice questions increase errors. Salmon (2006) notes parents tend to underestimate children's distress, especially when they were involved.
w: Leading yes/no questions produce inaccurate answers from children.
Repeating questions signals the first answer was wrong.
Multiple-choice questions push children to pick an option.
k: Use open-ended prompts with children, practised first on neutral events.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – Putting It in Practice 12.2

q: 'The door to children's feelings and memories locks from the inside' means:
o: We can only knock gently and hope the child trusts us enough to open
Children have no access to their memories until adolescence or adulthood
Interviewers must find ways to force disclosure when a child is reluctant
Parents hold the key
e: 'The door to children's feelings and memories locks from the inside' means we can only knock gently and hope the child trusts us enough to open it. Disclosure can't be forced or extracted, and pressure tends to close the door further. Investigative interviewing requires advanced education, training and supervision.
w: Children do have access to memories.
Forcing disclosure contradicts the metaphor: only the child can open the door.
Parents don't hold the key; the child does.
k: Children open up only when they trust you; you can't force disclosure.
h: Knock gently; they hold the key.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – Putting It in Practice 12.2

q: Familiar games like checkers or Uno provide assessment information through observing:
o: Setup, turn-taking, rule following, disappointment, strategy, and outcome
IQ and academic achievement compared with same-age peers in the classroom
Fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination only
Parental involvement
e: Familiar games like checkers or Uno provide rich assessment data by observing setup, turn-taking, rule following, handling disappointment, strategy and response to the outcome. Gardner's Mutual Storytelling Technique serves storytelling activities. The singed raccoon story warns about spontaneous games getting out of hand.
w: Games don't measure IQ or achievement.
Fine motor skills are a small part; social behaviour is the focus.
Parental involvement isn't what game play reveals here.
k: Board and card games reveal turn-taking, rule following, frustration tolerance and strategy.
h: Watch how they play the game.

q: Why say 'enough time to color one more picture' rather than '10 minutes left' to a young child?
o: Young children don't grasp linear time well, so concrete markers help
It sounds friendlier and keeps the child from feeling rushed or pressured
It extends the session so the child can finish whatever activity is underway
Children can't count
e: Young children don't grasp linear time well, so concrete markers such as 'enough time to color one more picture' help them understand how much time is left (Thompson and Henderson, 2007). Abstract minutes mean little to them, and concrete markers make the ending predictable and less abrupt.
w: Friendliness isn't the main reason; comprehension is.
It doesn't extend the session; it only makes the time concrete.
Some children can count; the issue is understanding time.
k: Use concrete time markers with young children; they don't grasp linear time.
h: One more picture, not ten minutes.

q: A resistant teen was rude all session. At closing the interviewer should:
o: Remain optimistic and empathic, avoiding anger or disappointment
Express disappointment so the teen learns consequences
Reprimand the behavior firmly before the teen leaves the office
Tell the parents
e: After a rude, resistant session, remain optimistic and empathic at closing, avoiding anger or disappointment. Countertransference urges to withdraw or punish are natural, but anger makes the teen less likely to seek help in the future, so the ending should leave the door open ('Termination as Motivation').
w: Expressing disappointment punishes and reduces future help-seeking.
Reprimanding pushes the teen further away.
Telling the parents about the rudeness breaches trust.
k: End sessions with resistant teens optimistically and empathically, not angrily.

q: Which is one of the four most important closing tasks with young people?
o: Reminding the client how caretakers will or won't be involved
Giving the child a diagnosis in simple, friendly terms
Assigning homework and reviewing it with the parents present in the room
Administering a brief standardized test of mood or behavior problems
e: Four key closing tasks with young people: summarize their problems, link problems to interventions, seek their positive involvement, and remind them how caretakers will or won't be involved. Examples include Beth's nightmares and Tommy's 'borrowing', where linking the problem to a concrete plan invited the child's cooperation.
w: Diagnosis isn't one of the four closing tasks.
Assigning homework isn't one of them.
Standardized testing isn't one of them.
k: Closing with youth: summarize, link problems to interventions, seek involvement, clarify caretaker involvement.
r: Sommers-Flanagan Ch12 – Summarizing, clarifying, seeking involvement

q: Asking 'Has our time together been like you thought it would be?' at the end serves to:
o: Empower the child by carefully sharing control
Test the child's memory for the session
Collect satisfaction feedback for the clinic's records
Diagnose the child's attitude to therapy
e: Asking 'Has our time together been like you thought it would be?' empowers the child by carefully sharing control. Children lack authority over much of their lives and respond well to choices and chances to ask questions or give their view.
w: It isn't a memory test; it invites the child's opinion.
It's about empowerment, not clinic records.
It isn't primarily diagnostic; it shares control.
k: Asking for the child's view at the end shares control and empowers them.

q: How do children's termination reactions differ from adults'?
o: In degree rather than substance – more overt and extreme
They have no reactions, since children don't attach to therapists
They are identical to adults' reactions in every respect
They are always positive, because children enjoy finishing therapy
e: Children's termination reactions differ from adults' in degree rather than substance: they feel the same loss and ambivalence, but express it more overtly and extremely, through hugs, tears, ugly looks, kicks or leaving early. The interviewer acts as observer, empathizer and gentle limit-setter during these endings.
w: Children do attach to therapists and react to endings.
They aren't identical; they're more overt.
They aren't always positive; many are sad or angry.
k: Children's termination reactions are like adults' but more overt and extreme.
